summary: Duolingo is more about maintaining streaks and less about true language mastery, but it's a fun way to keep engaged.
top_quotes: Duolingo is like, it's fun for keeping the streaks, you know? But really, it doesn't push me to the limits I need.
I think, sometimes I wish Duolingo was less about these daily goals and more about real conversations.
It's really just about the pride of seeing that number go up every day.

interview_script.question: Intro greeting
interview_script.answer: Hey, assalamu alaikum! It's Tariq here. How's it going? Excited to chat today!

interview_script.question: Short version of your life story?
interview_script.answer: So, basically, I grew up in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. My family is pretty big, lots of cousins and all. I moved to the UK for university, wanting to study engineering. It was a big culture shock at first, you know, with the weather and how people interact. But I love it now, especially getting to explore different cities and meet people from everywhere.

interview_script.question: Where did you grow up?
interview_script.answer: I grew up in Riyadh, which is the capital of Saudi Arabia. It's pretty much a bustling city, lots of modern stuff mixed with traditional Arabic culture.

interview_script.question: What was it like growing up there?
interview_script.answer: Growing up in Riyadh was, uh, it was interesting. You get a mix of old and new, like, you have the modern skyscrapers and malls, but also the traditional souks and family gatherings. It’s a big city, but it feels like home with familiar faces all around.

interview_script.question: One turning point in your life?
interview_script.answer: Moving to the UK for university was definitely a turning point. I mean, it was the first time I was really independent, you know? Having to manage everything myself, away from family and familiar settings. It was a bit overwhelming, but also exciting.

interview_script.question: Why was that a turning point?
interview_script.answer: Because it was when I realized how much I relied on my family for everything. Suddenly, I had to figure things out on my own, like cooking and budgeting, and even making new friends in a whole new country. It made me grow up quickly, in a way.

interview_script.question: How did you handle that situation?
interview_script.answer: I just took it one step at a time, you know? I reached out to other students, joined some societies, and tried not to overwhelm myself. I would call home when I felt lost, but also tried to handle things by experimenting and learning from mistakes.

interview_script.question: What do you care most about right now?
interview_script.answer: Right now, I'm really focused on perfecting my English and getting the best out of my studies here. I want to make sure that by the time I graduate, I'm really ready for the professional world, like with strong language skills and a good network.

interview_script.question: Why is that important?
interview_script.answer: Well, because English is the global language, right? And also, in engineering, communication is key. I want to make sure I can work anywhere and connect with people from all over. Plus, my career depends on how well I can adapt and express my ideas.

interview_script.question: What is a good day for you?
interview_script.answer: A good day is, I wake up early enough, get a bit of exercise in, head to class and actually understand what’s being taught. Then maybe later, grab coffee with friends or explore a new part of the city. Ending the day by catching up with family back home is perfect.

interview_script.question: What makes you say 'this was a good day'?
interview_script.answer: When I feel like I've achieved something, no matter how small. It could be understanding a tough topic in class or even just having a meaningful conversation with someone new. That feeling of progress, you know?

interview_script.question: How do you make big decisions?
interview_script.answer: I usually talk to my family first, especially my dad. He’s always been a guide for me. Then, I just weigh the pros and cons, try to imagine how each option will affect my future. Sometimes, I also ask friends for their opinions.

interview_script.question: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
interview_script.answer: I’m definitely more of a planner. I like to know what’s happening next, especially with my studies. But I try to leave some room for spontaneity, like, when friends come up with sudden plans.

interview_script.question: Example showing that?
interview_script.answer: Well, like when I first came to the UK, I had everything planned out – like flights, accommodation, even what I was going to study. But when a friend suggested a weekend trip to Scotland, I just went with it, even though it wasn’t in my plan. It was one of the best experiences I’ve had here.

interview_script.question: How do you handle risk?
interview_script.answer: I tend to be cautious with risks, especially when there’s a lot at stake, like my education or finances. I try to gather as much information as possible and see if the potential benefits really outweigh the risks.

interview_script.question: Typical weekday?
interview_script.answer: A typical weekday, I wake up early, around 7 am, grab a quick breakfast. Then it's off to university, where I have classes or labs until afternoon. I usually take a break for lunch with friends. After classes, I hit the library to study or work on assignments. In the evening, I try to relax a bit, maybe catch some Netflix or go for a run, and then I do a little Duolingo to keep that streak alive before bed.

interview_script.question: Which parts take the most energy?
interview_script.answer: Definitely the classes and labs. Especially when there’s a lot of technical content to absorb. Sometimes keeping up with everything can be draining, especially when there are deadlines looming.

interview_script.question: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
interview_script.answer: I wish I had more time for exploring new places in the UK or maybe picking up a new hobby. It feels like there's so much to see and do, but I get caught up with studies and daily routines.

interview_script.question: Biggest constraint last year?
interview_script.answer: Honestly, the biggest constraint was time management. Balancing studies, social life, and personal growth can be really challenging. Sometimes I feel like there's just not enough time in the day to do everything I want or need to.

interview_script.question: How do you deal with that constraint?
interview_script.answer: I started using calendars and setting reminders for everything. It helps me track deadlines and make sure I’m allocating enough time to each task. Also, learning to say no to things that aren't a priority helped a lot.

interview_script.question: People you feel closest to?
interview_script.answer: My family, for sure. Even though I'm far away, we talk almost every day. And my best friends from back home. Here, I've made a couple of close friends who feel like family now, which is comforting.

interview_script.question: Describe those relationships.
interview_script.answer: With my family, it’s very open and supportive. We share everything. My friends back home are like brothers, you know? We grew up together. Here, it's more like, we support each other because we’re all in the same boat, away from home.

interview_script.question: Where do you spend most of your time?
interview_script.answer: Probably at university, between classes, the library, and some campus events. But I also spend a lot of time in my flat, you know, studying or just chilling.

interview_script.question: How do you feel in those spaces?
interview_script.answer: At university, I feel motivated and, um, focused. It's where I know I'm working towards my goals. At home, it's more relaxed. It’s my safe space where I can just be myself and recharge.

interview_script.question: What makes you feel that way?
interview_script.answer: The energy at university is very driven, with everyone working hard, it's contagious. And at home, I've made it cozy, with reminders of family around which makes it comforting.

interview_script.question: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
interview_script.answer: Usually my family first, and then close friends. My dad gives the best advice, and my mom, she knows exactly how to make me feel better. My friends here are also great for more immediate issues, like if I need someone to talk to right away.

interview_script.question: One tough moment in the last year?
interview_script.answer: There was a time when I was really struggling with an important project at university. It was overwhelming, and I didn’t know if I could finish it on time. Combine that with a bit of homesickness, and it was tough.

interview_script.question: How did it affect you?
interview_script.answer: I felt really stressed and kind of isolated, even though there were people around to help. It made me question if I was cut out for this, you know? Like, maybe I took on too much by studying abroad.

interview_script.question: How did you cope?
interview_script.answer: I reached out to my university’s support services and they helped a lot. I also started managing my time better and took more breaks to avoid burnout. Talking to friends and family helped me see that it’s okay to struggle and ask for help.

interview_script.question: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
interview_script.answer: Taking a step back and doing something completely different, like going for a walk or watching a movie. Also, writing things down helps me organize my thoughts and see things more clearly.

interview_script.question: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
interview_script.answer: In a few years, I hope to be working in a field I love, hopefully in a place that excites me. I want to have a good work-life balance, be able to travel, and maybe pursue other passions, like photography.

interview_script.question: What do you want to be different?
interview_script.answer: I would like to be more fluent in English – not just mastering the language, but being more confident in using it. I also want to be better at managing stress and not let it control me.

interview_script.question: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
interview_script.answer: Before Duolingo, I mostly relied on formal classes and textbooks. I also tried to watch English movies and read books. It was effective to some extent, but it was hard to stay motivated, and sometimes I felt like I wasn’t really absorbing the language naturally.

interview_script.question: Most annoying part of old method?
interview_script.answer: The lack of interaction was definitely annoying. With textbooks and classes, you rarely get to practice speaking or listening in real-world scenarios. It felt too theoretical, without much practical application.

interview_script.question: Time it really failed?
interview_script.answer: One time, I was trying to talk to a tourist at a café back home, and I realized I didn’t know how to respond to half of what they were saying, despite all my studying. It was frustrating because I thought I knew the language better than that.

interview_script.question: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: I think it was from a friend who mentioned they were using it to learn Spanish. They seemed pretty hooked, so I thought I’d give it a try for English.

interview_script.question: What convinced you to try it?
interview_script.answer: The idea of a game-like app was appealing, you know? And they said it was free, so I figured there was nothing to lose. Plus, the idea of improving my language skills at my own pace sounded good.

interview_script.question: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
interview_script.answer: Sure, so I open the app, and it usually shows me where I left off. I’m sort of competitive with myself, always want to keep the streak going. So, I start with some exercises, usually a mix of translating sentences and using the words in context. There's always that bird reminding me about how many days I've been on track. Sometimes, I do the speaking exercises, but it feels a bit silly talking to my phone. I also like the little animations and sounds when I get something right; it’s satisfying.

interview_script.question: Most helpful part?
interview_script.answer: The reminders are actually pretty helpful. They keep me in check, making sure I don’t slack off. Also, the way they introduce new words with related sentences helps me remember them better.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part?
interview_script.answer: Sometimes, the exercises feel too repetitive and not challenging enough. Like, I wish there was more focus on real-life conversation skills or, um, more advanced vocabulary. It feels like I’m not progressing past a certain point.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
interview_script.answer: Definitely when I encounter sentences that don't make sense in real life. It's like I'm learning things that I might never actually use. It can feel a bit pointless sometimes, you know?

interview_script.question: One time that frustration showed up?
interview_script.answer: Recently, there was this sentence about, I don’t know, something about a cat wearing shoes? It was funny, but I thought, 'When am I ever going to use this?' It made me question if I was wasting time on these lessons.

interview_script.question: Do you use workarounds?
interview_script.answer: Sometimes, I look for conversation groups or language exchange meetups online to practice. Or even watching English TV shows with subtitles helps more with understanding real dialogue.

interview_script.question: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
interview_script.answer: They give me a chance to use the language in real, practical situations. It's more about speaking naturally and understanding the flow of conversation, which is something Duolingo lacks.

interview_script.question: Worst-case scenario in this space?
interview_script.answer: Worst-case would be spending all this time and not seeing any real improvement in my English. Like, if I couldn't communicate effectively in a job interview or something important, it would really undermine all the effort I'm putting in.

interview_script.question: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
interview_script.answer: I hope it challenges me and helps me learn new things that I can actually use. And, of course, I just want to maintain my streak. It’s a bit of a pride thing now.

interview_script.question: How do you know Duolingo worked?
interview_script.answer: I guess when I can recall a word I learned on the app in a normal conversation. Or when I hear something in a movie and think, 'Oh, we covered that recently.'

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: I would put more focus on real-life conversation skills and maybe have more levels for advanced learners. It should feel progressive rather than just repetitive.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
interview_script.answer: I think there should be more integration between digital learning and real-world practice. Like, maybe apps having partnerships with conversational clubs or platforms to facilitate real interactions.

interview_script.question: Anything important we didn't cover?
interview_script.answer: I think we’ve covered a lot! Maybe just that language learning is, um, quite personal, you know? What works for someone might not work for another. I guess patience and persistence are key.

interview_script.question: Permission to build a digital twin?
interview_script.answer: Yeah, sure. I mean, if it helps improve the app or user experience, why not?
